items.title: Monitoring That Watches People
items.stakes: A room nobody could hear for nineteen days, on a dashboard that stayed green.
items.reward: Monitoring that tests what people experience, and alerts that reach someone who can act.

items.title: Green for nineteen days.
items.body: For nineteen days the dashboard asked every device in Room 3 one question — are you there? — and every device said yes. Nothing asked whether anyone on the far end could hear the room. People in the room noticed something was off and quietly used a laptop microphone; nobody reported it. Maya pulls last quarter's incident log: of eighty-four incidents, sixty-one — 73% — were first reported by a user. The users were the monitoring.
items.label: Test: how many meetings — and why the dashboard stayed green.

items.alt: A 21-day timeline for Lagos Room 3: ‘devices answer’ green every day; ‘room can be heard’ red for 19 days — ceiling mics muted; ‘synthetic test’ — none. Last quarter, 61 of 84 incidents (73%) were first reported by users.
items.caption: The users were the monitoring.

items.title: ‘PRIVACY: ceiling mics off · recall: never’
items.body: The DSP preset list for Room 3: ‘PRIVACY — ceiling mics off. Auto-recall of NORMAL: never.’ Somebody made it for one confidential meeting three years ago and every room inherited it.

options.label: The same device checks, more often
options.result: Every device answers every minute. Room 3 would still have been green.
options.consequence: Faster answers to the wrong question.

options.label: A synthetic test call in every empty room every 30 minutes — join, a tone out through the speakers and back through the mics, the far end, captions present — built on the monitoring platform, with a runbook for a failed test
options.result: Galen builds it in two weeks. On day three it catches a dead amplifier in Oslo fourteen minutes after it fails.

options.result: Reports arrive faster — when people bother.

options.result: Some do. Room 3 would have been caught on day six.

items.title: The canary
items.body: For most of the twentieth century, British coal miners carried canaries underground. The birds reacted to carbon monoxide long before the miners could, so a canary in distress was a warning to get out. The last pit canaries were retired in 1986, replaced by electronic detectors. The canary didn't measure the mine's machinery. It measured the one thing that mattered — whether the air could keep someone alive.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #117 · AVERY'S LENS  Monitor what people experience  A device that answers a ping can still be a room nobody can hear. Test the outcome — can a meeting start, can both ends hear, are captions on — and send the alert to a role that can act.  Every device in a room was green for nineteen days while nobody on the far end could hear it.

items.title: Every thirty minutes.
items.body: The tests run every thirty minutes in every room that isn't booked. A failure can start at any moment between two tests, so on average it waits half the interval: t̄ = T ÷ 2 = 15 minutes, and never more than 30. Room 3's nineteen days would have been fourteen minutes. And when a test fails at 2 a.m., it doesn't wake the architect: it goes to the EMEA on-call engineer on the rota, with a runbook for exactly that alert.
items.label: Test: the average wait — and the new user-reported share.

items.prompt: The tests work. When one fails, who finds out?

items.title: ‘source: user · user · user · monitor · user’
items.body: The incident log's ‘first reported by’ column, scrolled end to end: user, user, user, monitor, user, user… Sixty-one of eighty-four. The monitoring had been thorough about the wrong question.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  A green dashboard can hide a room nobody can hear. Monitor outcomes, not devices: a synthetic test call in every empty room — join, audio both ways, captions — on a schedule you choose knowing a failure waits on average half the interval (t̄ = T ÷ 2). Send each alert to the on-call role that can act, with a runbook, and track one number: the share of incidents users find first. When it falls, the monitoring is working.
